subject: Performance SLO qualification - Nova Retail
messages:

Subject: Re: Performance SLO qualification - Nova Retail

Hi Marissa / Neha,

Thanks again for the call this morning — helpful discussion. Quick recap from our side and a few clarifying points so we can move faster on an estimate/proof-of-concept: 

Summary of target SLOs (what we care most about):
- Time-to-first-token (TTFT) for streaming responses: <= 150 ms (P95).
- End-to-last-token for typical answers (~150 tokens): <= 800 ms (P95).
- Sustained concurrency: 200 concurrent active streams, with ability to spike to 1,000 for marketing events.
- Throughput: roughly 20k tokens/sec sustained across fleet (peak 50k tokens/sec).
- Model behavior: streaming is required for UX; we will send mostly short prompts (avg 40 tokens) but occasionally longer generation.

Main constraints:
- Budget guidance: we're targeting a production unit cost that keeps cost-per-capable-session reasonable — ask you to call out levers (batching/quant, model variants) that materially change unit economics.
- Security/regulatory: data stays in our AWS account for the POC; we may need Private deployment later.

Next asks from Nova Retail:
1) Rough sizing and cost brackets for a POC that hits the SLOs above.
2) Short list of concrete levers you'd test during a performance spike (e.g., batching windows, prefix caching, quantization levels, model variants).
3) Suggested next steps and timeline for a small POC (2 weeks) to validate end-to-end.

I attached the SLO worksheet we started — it has some traffic shape numbers. Maya (cc'd) will own the POC on our side.

Appreciate it — could you reply with a quick plan by EOD Tuesday?

— Tom
Product Lead, Nova Retail

From: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwoodinference.com>

Date: Mon, 03 May 2027 09:25:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Performance SLO qualification - Nova Retail

Tom — thanks for the clear recap and the worksheet. Here's a concise plan that answers your three asks and outlines the levers we'd evaluate in a 2-week POC. I'll keep it actionable so your engineering team can map to it quickly.

1) Sizing & cost brackets (POC scope: validate P95 streaming TTFT <=150ms, 200 sustained concurrency, spike to 1k):
- Option A (Baseline Hosted): use our hosted nodes with autoscaling — good for speed to value. Expected baseline cost: medium; estimated for POC (2 weeks): ~$12k–$18k depending on traffic spikes.
- Option B (Dedicated small cluster): reserved pool of GPU instances (better predictability). POC estimate: ~$9k–$14k (includes reserved capacity + short-term burst).
- Option C (Private evaluation in your AWS account): depends on infra; we'll provide sizing and AMI. POC infra spend estimated: ~$7k–$12k (compute only), plus Redwood engineer time.

2) Concrete levers we'll test (priority order):
- Continuous batching & dynamic batching windows: reduces per-token cost by increasing batching for short prompts while keeping TTFT under SLO. We'll tune max-wait and max-batch-size per traffic shape.
- Prefix / KV caching: cache repeated prefixes and statically repeated system prompts to avoid repeated computation. Quick wins for sessionized chat.
- Model variants & multi-model routing: route low-latency short prompts to a smaller, faster variant; route long-form or high-quality responses to the larger model.
- Quantization profiles: evaluate int8 and mixed-precision paths (q4_0/ q8_0 equivalents) to reduce memory footprint and improve throughput. Measure quality delta on your prompts.
- Streaming token priority & early-first-token optimizations: prioritize generating the first token quickly (TTFT) and stream remaining tokens while batching for backend efficiency.
- Autoscaling & burst pools: combine a smaller reserved baseline with a burstable pool to cover marketing spikes.

3) POC steps & timeline (2-week plan):
- Day 0–2: Kickoff, ingest SLO worksheet, confirm traffic shape and sample prompts; grant sandbox infra access (for Private option) or define traffic replay for Hosted.
- Day 3–6: Baseline measurement (current Hosted baseline or quick emulation) + initial tuning (batching and cache).
- Day 7–10: Quantization and model-variant experiments; measure quality regression on your eval set.
- Day 11–13: Spike testing, concurrency ramps to 1k, validate TTFT P95 and end-to-end latencies.
- Day 14: Results review, recommendation (config for production), and next steps (Dedicated sizing or Private deployment plan).

Deliverables: SLO test report, cost/throughput tradeoff matrix, recommended config (batching params, quant profile, routing policy), and a short playbook for production rollout.

Attachments: SLO-tech-summary.pdf (short tech note describing the levers above).

Next steps: I'm available for a 30-min follow-up Wednesday (May 5) 10–11am PDT or Thursday 9–10am PDT. If one of those works, I'll send a calendar invite and a short prework doc so we can lock down sample prompts and access.

If useful I can also loop Eng (Rishi) to do a quick architecture session on Day 1.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference

Thanks Marissa — that plan looks good. Quick clarifications from our infra side:
- For spike testing we can provide traffic replay and a short window where we route live traffic (we prefer not to send production data into hosted environments).
- Quality: we need max 1.5% drop in key intent-classification accuracy when trying quantized models. Will share a small eval set by EOD Thursday.
- Can you ballpark the delta in latency if we move from int8 to mixed-precision? Also curious if prefix caching will materialize for our mostly session-based flows.

We're fine with Wed 5/5 10am PDT — confirm and send the invite.

— Maya

Perfect — invite sent for Wed 5/5 10–10:30am PDT. A few quick answers so your team can prep:

- Latency delta by quant profile (very rough guidance; we'll measure on your eval prompts):
  • float32 / fp16 baseline: best quality, baseline latency.
  • mix-precision (fp16 + kernel optimizations): ~5–10% throughput gain and small latency improvements vs fp32.
  • int8 / high-quant paths: often 1.8–2.5x throughput improvement depending on model architecture and kernel availability; latency per token can drop ~20–40% in favorable cases, but results are workload-dependent.

- Prefix caching: for session-based flows where many interactions reuse system prompt or several repeated prefixes, prefix/KV caching frequently yields 30–70% reduction in repeated compute for subsequent messages. For Nova's traffic shape (sessionized), we expect meaningful wins.

- For the POC we'll provide: a short config matrix with concrete values to test (batching max-wait 5–15ms, max-batch-size 32–128, cache TTL options), and a quick quality checklist for quant experiments.

I'll have Rishi on the call to go deeper into kernel/path tradeoffs. See you Wednesday.

— Marissa
Senior Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
